--- title: "July PCE Held at 3.7% as Jackson Hole Opens: The Fed's Gauge Did Not Cool" pagetitle: "July PCE Held at 3.7% as Jackson Hole Opens: The Fed's Gauge Did Not Cool" date: "2026-08-28" author: Yoram Gilboa categories: [economics, inflation, federal reserve, data visualization, labor market] description: "Real household spending barely budged, yearly core inflation stayed stuck, and Polymarket still split a September hold from a hike." image: figures/pce-headline-core-yoy.png image-alt: "Headline and core PCE year-over-year inflation since 2023, with the Fed 2% target" toc: true toc-location: right code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" format: html: title-prefix: "" --- The Bureau of Economic Analysis ([BEA]{title="Bureau of Economic Analysis"}) is the federal statistical agency that measures US income and spending. Its July report on Personal Consumption Expenditures ([PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"}) showed that the price index the Federal Reserve targets rose **\+0\.2%** from June and **3\.7%** from a year earlier. Core [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"}, which excludes food and energy, also rose **\+0\.2%** and held at **3\.3%** year over year. The yearly rates did not move. Two days later Chair Warsh opened Jackson Hole with that print still on the table. The 9/15/2026\-9/16/2026 [FOMC]{title="Federal Open Market Committee"} meeting is next. This post stays with the tables. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Reproducing this analysis Expand any chart block for the Python. Run from this post folder: `01_fetch_data.py`, then `02_clean_data.py`, then `03_visualizations.py`, then `04_compute_stats.py`. [FRED]{title="Federal Reserve Economic Data"} series and the [BEA]{title="Bureau of Economic Analysis"} release are listed under Methodology. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## How to read this print Rest the pointer on short names such as [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} or [BEA]{title="Bureau of Economic Analysis"} to see the full phrase. Personal Consumption Expenditures are what households spend on goods and services. The [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} price index tracks those prices. Core [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} excludes food and energy. Disposable personal income, or [DPI]{title="Disposable Personal Income"}, is income after taxes. The personal saving rate is saving as a share of [DPI]{title="Disposable Personal Income"}. The Federal Reserve's dual mandate is maximum employment and stable prices. The Fed's 2% inflation goal is defined on [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"}, not on the Consumer Price Index ([CPI]{title="Consumer Price Index"}). [CPI]{title="Consumer Price Index"} is built by the Bureau of Labor Statistics from an urban consumer basket. [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} is built by the [BEA]{title="Bureau of Economic Analysis"} from a broader set of spending, including more services, and it updates weights with actual spending shares. That is why a [CPI]{title="Consumer Price Index"} print and a [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} print for the same month can differ without either series being wrong. The funds rate is a nominal rate, before inflation. The real policy rate, written [r]{title="the actual short-term real interest rate: the funds rate after inflation"}, is that same overnight rate after inflation. [r\*]{title="an estimated short-term real interest rate that would neither add demand nor take it away"} is a different number: an estimate of where r would sit if policy were neither adding demand nor taking it away. If r sat at r\*, cheap credit would not be pushing inflation higher, and expensive credit would not be squeezing hiring. Nobody prints r\* the way the [BEA]{title="Bureau of Economic Analysis"} prints [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"}. Staffs and markets estimate it; this post does not. ::: ::: {#60444123 .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The third card is a quantity, not a price. The [BEA]{title="Bureau of Economic Analysis"} said the inflation-adjusted volume of household spending, often called real spending or real [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"}, rose 1\.3 billion dollars in July. That is under 0\.1% from June, so the card treats the month as essentially flat even though the dollar change is not zero. Personal income rose **\+0\.4%** in July, and disposable personal income rose **\+0\.5%**. Current-dollar [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} rose **\+0\.2%**, or 36\.3 billion dollars, as services gained 86\.2 billion and goods fell 49\.9 billion. Personal saving was **3\.0%** of [DPI]{title="Disposable Personal Income"}. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Already on this blog The funds target is **3\.50% to 3\.75%**. The July [FOMC]{title="Federal Open Market Committee"} held **9\-3**, with 3 dissents preferring a 25 basis-point increase. July payrolls fell **\-23k** and unemployment was **4\.1%**. Headline [CPI]{title="Consumer Price Index"} rose **\+0\.1%** on the month and **3\.4%** year over year. Core [CPI]{title="Consumer Price Index"} rose **\+0\.2%** and **2\.5%**, while [PPI]{title="Producer Price Index"} final demand was unchanged on the month. ::: ## The Fed's preferred gauge did not cool Year-over-year headline [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} stayed at **3\.7%**, the same as June, while core [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} stayed at **3\.3%**. July's monthly headline and core prints were both **\+0\.2%**. June's softer headline month did not pull the yearly rate down. Headline inflation peaked at 4\.1% during the spring energy spike. The Fed's 2% goal is a [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} target. [CPI]{title="Consumer Price Index"} looked cooler in July because the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the [BEA]{title="Bureau of Economic Analysis"} use different baskets and weights. ::: {#cell-fig-pce-headline-core-yoy .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # YoY means this month versus the same month last year. July did not change that yearly picture, even after the spring energy spike faded. ## Monthly prints still run above a 2% path A yearly rate can hide a friendly month. June headline [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} prices fell **\-0\.1%**. July went back to **\+0\.2%** for both headline and core. A useful benchmark is the monthly pace that compounds to 2% over a year, about **0\.2%** a month. July's 0\.2% prints sit above that line. One month above the line does not lock in a high yearly rate, and one month below it (June headline) does not lock in 2%. The last 12 months show several readings well above that dashed path, then June's dip, then July back above it. ::: {#cell-fig-pce-monthly-pace .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot = df.loc[:, ["pce_headline_mom", "pce_core_mom"]].dropna().iloc[-12:] x = np.arange(len(plot)) width = 0.38 fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.2)) ax.bar(x - width / 2, plot["pce_headline_mom"], width=width, color=COLORS["headline"], edgecolor="white", label="Headline PCE") ax.bar(x + width / 2, plot["pce_core_mom"], width=width, color=COLORS["core"], edgecolor="white", label="Core PCE") ax.axhline(TWO_PCT_MONTHLY, color=COLORS["target"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1.0) ax.text( 0.02, 0.92, "Dashed line: monthly pace that compounds to 2%", color=COLORS["target"], fontsize=8, transform=ax.transAxes, ) ax.axhline(0, color=COLORS["neutral"], linewidth=0.8) tick_idx = list(range(0, len(plot), 2)) if (len(plot) - 1) not in tick_idx: tick_idx.append(len(plot) - 1) ax.set_xticks([x[i] for i in tick_idx]) ax.set_xticklabels([plot.index[i].strftime("%b\n%y") for i in tick_idx]) ax.set_ylabel("Month-over-month (%)") ax.set_xlabel("Month") ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=8) plt.tight_layout() fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "pce-monthly-pace.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Grouped monthly headline and core PCE changes for the last 12 months, with a dashed line equal to the monthly pace that compounds to 2% a year.](index_files/figure-html/fig-pce-monthly-pace-output-1.png){#fig-pce-monthly-pace width=759 height=393} ::: ::: ::: {.figure-source} Source: [BEA](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-july-2026) via FRED series PCEPI and PCEPILFE. ::: June's headline decline did not persist. July put both measures back above the monthly pace that compounds to 2%, a benchmark rather than a forecast. ## Real spending was flat while saving ticked up "Real spending" means the volume of goods and services households bought after stripping out price changes. If prices rise 0.2% and households spend 0.2% more dollars, real spending is unchanged: they paid more for the same basket. The third card's 1\.3 billion dollars is that volume change in July, which the [BEA]{title="Bureau of Economic Analysis"} also described as under 0\.1% month over month. Compared with a year earlier, real spending was still 2\.1% higher. That yearly gap can stay positive even when the latest month adds almost nothing. The two facts are not a contradiction. They answer different questions: the yearly number asks whether the level of consumption is above last summer; the monthly number asks whether households added more volume in July itself. July's answer to the second question is no. That is why this print is not an overheating boom in volumes. It is a pause in the quantity of spending while prices keep rising. The saving rate was **3\.0%** of disposable income, up from 2\.6% in June but still a thin cushion. ::: {#cell-fig-real-pce-saving .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot = df.loc["2023-01-01":, ["real_pce_yoy", "saving_rate"]].dropna() fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots( 2, 1, figsize=(8.0, 7.0), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2.2, 1.4]} ) ax1.plot(plot.index, plot["real_pce_yoy"], color=COLORS["target"], linewidth=1.9) ax2.plot(plot.index, plot["saving_rate"], color=COLORS["core"], linewidth=1.8) july = pd.Timestamp("2026-07-01") if july in plot.index: ax2.scatter(july, plot.loc[july, "saving_rate"], s=40, color=COLORS["core"], edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.8, zorder=5) ax2.text(july, plot.loc[july, "saving_rate"] + 0.18, f" July {plot.loc[july, 'saving_rate']:.1f}%", color=COLORS["core"], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", va="bottom") extend_xlim(ax1, plot.index, 0.22) ax1.set_ylabel("Real PCE YoY (%)") ax2.set_ylabel("Saving rate (%)") ax2.set_xlabel("Month") ax2.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator()) ax2.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y")) plt.tight_layout() fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "real-pce-saving.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Stacked panels separate real PCE year-over-year growth from the personal saving rate; the latest saving-rate print is marked in the lower panel.](index_files/figure-html/fig-real-pce-saving-output-1.png){#fig-real-pce-saving width=759 height=663} ::: ::: ::: {.figure-source} Source: FRED series DPCERA3M086SBEA (real PCE) and PSAVERT (personal saving rate); July saving rate aligned to the BEA release. ::: ## Labor context: a weak July jobs print The dual mandate also covers employment. Nonfarm payrolls fell **\-23k** in July while unemployment held at **4\.1%**. That mix can look calmer than it is. The unemployment rate is jobless people divided by the labor force, not by the whole adult population. If people leave the labor force, the denominator shrinks and the rate can stay near 4\.1% even as fewer adults are working or looking. The participation rate, the share of adults in the labor force, was 61\.4% in July, versus 62\.1% in January (\-0\.7 percentage points). The jobs print is therefore a weaker market and a smaller labor force, not a clean all-clear on the employment side of the mandate. ::: {#cell-fig-labor-dashboard .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Two panels keep payroll thousands off the unemployment-rate scale. # The July payroll label sits under the orange bar with no extra marker. plot = df.loc["2025-01-01":"2026-07-01", ["payroll_change_k", "unrate"]].dropna() payroll_average = plot["payroll_change_k"].rolling(3).mean() fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots( 2, 1, figsize=(8.0, 7.0), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2.2, 1.4]} ) bar_colors = [COLORS["target"] if v >= 0 else COLORS["headline"] for v in plot["payroll_change_k"]] ax1.bar(plot.index, plot["payroll_change_k"], width=20, color=bar_colors, alpha=0.75, edgecolor="white") ax1.plot(plot.index, payroll_average, color=COLORS["core"], linewidth=2.0) ax1.axhline(0, color=COLORS["neutral"], linewidth=0.8) ax2.plot(plot.index, plot["unrate"], color=COLORS["headline"], linewidth=1.9) july = pd.Timestamp("2026-07-01") if july in plot.index: val = float(plot.loc[july, "payroll_change_k"]) un = float(plot.loc[july, "unrate"]) pad = max(12.0, abs(plot["payroll_change_k"]).max() * 0.06) ax1.text(july, val - pad, f"July {val:+.0f}k", color=COLORS["headline"], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", ha="center", va="top", zorder=6) ax2.text(july, un, f" {un:.1f}%", color=COLORS["headline"], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", va="center") extend_xlim(ax1, plot.index, 0.10) ax1.set_ylabel("Monthly payroll change (thousands)") ax2.set_ylabel("Unemployment rate (%)") ax2.set_xlabel("Month") ax1.yaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.StrMethodFormatter("{x:,.0f}")) ax1.legend( handles=[ Patch(facecolor=COLORS["target"], edgecolor="white", label="Payroll gain (top panel)"), Patch(facecolor=COLORS["headline"], edgecolor="white", label="Payroll loss (top panel)"), plt.Line2D([0], [0], color=COLORS["core"], linewidth=2.0, label="3-month payroll average"), ], loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=8, ) ax2.legend( handles=[plt.Line2D([0], [0], color=COLORS["headline"], linewidth=1.9, label="Unemployment rate (bottom panel)")], loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=8, ) solid_right_spine(ax1) solid_right_spine(ax2) ax2.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator(interval=3)) ax2.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b\n%Y")) plt.tight_layout() fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "labor-dashboard.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Top panel: monthly payroll gains and losses plus a three-month average. Bottom panel: the unemployment rate. Each panel has its own axis and its own legend.](index_files/figure-html/fig-labor-dashboard-output-1.png){#fig-labor-dashboard width=759 height=662} ::: ::: ::: {.figure-source} Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics via FRED series PAYEMS, UNRATE, and CIVPART. ::: ## The policy rate and core PCE are different questions The [FOMC]{title="Federal Open Market Committee"} does not pick a single overnight rate. It sets a target range for the federal funds rate, the overnight interest rate banks charge one another to borrow reserves. The current range is 3\.50% to 3\.75%. That 25-basis-point band is the instruction: overnight trading is supposed to stay inside it. The Fed uses its overnight facilities to keep the effective rate in the band. The chart plots the upper edge of that range, 3\.75%. Core [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} is 3\.3% year over year. That is how fast prices in the core household basket rose over twelve months. It is a price change, not an interest rate. Putting the funds ceiling and core inflation in one subtracted "gap" makes them look like a single tightness score. They are not. ::: {#cell-fig-fed-funds-core-pce .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot = df.loc["2023-01-01":, ["fed_target_upper", "pce_core_yoy"]].dropna() fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots( 2, 1, figsize=(8.0, 7.0), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.4, 2.2]} ) ax1.plot(plot.index, plot["fed_target_upper"], color=COLORS["core"], linewidth=1.9) ax2.plot(plot.index, plot["pce_core_yoy"], color=COLORS["headline"], linewidth=1.9) ax2.axhline(2.0, color=COLORS["target"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1.0, alpha=0.7) ax2.text(plot.index[4], 2.12, "Fed 2% PCE target", color=COLORS["target"], fontsize=8, alpha=0.85) last = plot.iloc[-1] ax1.text(plot.index[-1], last["fed_target_upper"], f" {last['fed_target_upper']:.2f}%", color=COLORS["core"], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", va="center") ax2.text(plot.index[-1], last["pce_core_yoy"], f" {last['pce_core_yoy']:.1f}%", color=COLORS["headline"], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", va="center") extend_xlim(ax1, plot.index, 0.18) ax1.set_ylabel("Fed funds upper bound (%)") ax2.set_ylabel("Core PCE, year-over-year (%)") ax2.set_xlabel("Month") funds = plot["fed_target_upper"] ax1.set_ylim(float(funds.min()) - 0.40, float(funds.max()) + 0.25) ax2.set_ylim(0, float(plot["pce_core_yoy"].max()) + 0.4) ax2.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator()) ax2.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y")) plt.tight_layout() fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fed-funds-core-pce.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Top panel: the upper bound of the federal funds target range. Bottom panel: core PCE year-over-year inflation with the 2% goal. These are two published series, not an estimate of r\*.](index_files/figure-html/fig-fed-funds-core-pce-output-1.png){#fig-fed-funds-core-pce width=759 height=663} ::: ::: ::: {.figure-source} Source: Federal Reserve (DFEDTARU) and BEA via FRED (PCEPILFE). ::: A policy rate in the mid-3s and core inflation in the mid-3s can coexist without telling you whether policy is tight or easy. Tight or easy is a comparison of two different real rates. The real policy rate, [r]{title="the actual short-term real interest rate: the funds rate after inflation"}, is the funds rate after inflation. [r\*]{title="an estimated short-term real interest rate that would neither add demand nor take it away"} is an estimate of where r would sit if policy were neither adding demand nor taking it away. If r sat at r\*, monetary policy would not be pushing the economy to heat up or cool down. If r is above r\*, policy is pulling demand down. If r is below r\*, it is adding demand. r\* is not in any official table. It has to be estimated, and estimates disagree. This chart does not produce r or r\*, and it also leaves out financial conditions and the rest of the dual mandate. Chair Warsh's prepared Jackson Hole remarks kept [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} at the center of the price-stability discussion without turning this post into a speech recap: > "And while this summer's PCE and CPI readings were better than expected, they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved." > > Source: [Kevin Warsh, Jackson Hole, 8/28/2026](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/warsh20260828a.htm) That line matches the tables: July brought no further cooldown in the yearly rates. ## Putting it together Yearly headline and core [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} did not cool. They held at **3\.7%** and **3\.3%**. June's \-0\.1% headline dip did not persist; July was \+0\.2% on both headline and core. Payrolls fell \-23k while unemployment held at 4\.1%, with participation lower than in January. ### What it means for **Fed path.** The dual mandate is split. July [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} alone did not clear the inflation side, while softer payrolls and a smaller labor force raised the employment concern. This post makes no rate call. As of 8/29/2026, [Polymarket](https://polymarket.com/event/fed-decision-in-september-762) priced a September hold at 54\.5% and a 25 basis-point increase at 43\.5%. Those are wagers, not a forecast from this analysis. **Households.** Nominal income and [DPI]{title="Disposable Personal Income"} rose, but real spending was flat and the saving rate is only 3\.0% of disposable income. That is a thin buffer if hours or prices worsen. **Investors.** This is not a new inflation spike, and it is not an easing signal. June's monthly dip now has a counter-observation. ## What to watch next The 9/4/2026 employment report is the next labor checkpoint, including participation as well as the unemployment rate. The 9/15/2026\-9/16/2026 [FOMC]{title="Federal Open Market Committee"} includes new projections, and August [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} follows on 9/30/2026. Watch whether monthly core inflation remains near 0\.2%. One month will not set policy by itself. ## Limitations Monthly [PCE]{title="Personal Consumption Expenditures"} estimates are seasonally adjusted and revise, while yearly rates move slowly. [FRED]{title="Federal Reserve Economic Data"} carried the July series used here, so no history was reconstructed. Dollar figures come from the [BEA]{title="Bureau of Economic Analysis"} release. The policy-rate and core-inflation panels are not an [r\*]{title="an estimated short-term real interest rate that would neither add demand nor take it away"} estimate. Polymarket odds move by the hour and are recorded as of 8/29/2026. The official Warsh quotation is context rather than evidence about the tables. One month does not determine September policy. ## Methodology and data | Series or table | Use in this post | Source | |---|---|---| | PCEPI | Headline PCE price index, m/m and y/y | [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCEPI) / [BEA](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-july-2026) | | PCEPILFE | Core PCE price index | [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCEPILFE) | | DPCERA3M086SBEA | Real PCE quantity index | [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DPCERA3M086SBEA) | | PSAVERT | Personal saving rate | [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PSAVERT) | | PAYEMS, UNRATE, CIVPART | Payrolls, unemployment, participation | [BLS via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/) | | DFEDTARU | Fed funds target upper bound | [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU) | | Personal Income and Outlays | Official July dollar and percent prints | [BEA July 2026 PIO](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-july-2026) | | Fed Decision in September? | Hold vs 25 bp hike odds | [Polymarket](https://polymarket.com/event/fed-decision-in-september-762) | | Jackson Hole remarks | One short blockquote | [Warsh remarks](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/warsh20260828a.htm) | : Public data used in the analysis. ### How this post was built The Python code for each chart is in this post. Expand a chart block to see it. The pipeline runs in numeric order from the post folder: - `scripts/01_fetch_data.py` downloads the [FRED]{title="Federal Reserve Economic Data"} series, including CIVPART for participation. - `scripts/02_clean_data.py` computes month-over-month and year-over-year changes. Official July [BEA]{title="Bureau of Economic Analysis"} rates are pinned to the release if FRED rounding differs. - `scripts/03_visualizations.py` writes the five PNGs under `figures/`. - `scripts/04_compute_stats.py` writes every prose and card value to `stats/summary_stats.json`. pandas handles the tables and matplotlib draws the figures. Official [BEA]{title="Bureau of Economic Analysis"} dollar figures that FRED does not publish as standalone monthly series are entered from the [Personal Income and Outlays release](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-july-2026) and marked in `04_compute_stats.py`. --- *Data current as of 8/29/2026. BEA Personal Income and Outlays for July 2026 was released 8/26/2026\. Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole remarks were delivered 8/28/2026\.*
